paragraphs: AnyEdit addresses a difficulty in updating language models: changing a short fact is different from changing a complete poem, code snippet, or mathematical derivation. The paper attributes existing methods’ difficulties with longer material to their reliance on modifying a single token’s hidden state. It calls this restriction an efficacy barrier.

The proposed approach breaks the desired knowledge into sequential chunks and edits a key token within each chunk in turn. This makes editing an autoregressive process, with multiple coordinated updates supporting a longer output. AnyEdit also acts as a framework around existing editing methods, extending the lengths and formats they can address.

The authors ground the approach in the Chain Rule of Mutual Information, presenting a theoretical argument for its ability to update arbitrary knowledge. Their experiments report a 21.5% improvement over strong baselines across UnKEBench, AKEW, and the new EditEverything dataset. These findings support sequential editing as a way to broaden knowledge updates beyond isolated short answers.
icml-2025-anyedit-edit-any-knowledge-enc.tldr: AnyEdit updates long, varied knowledge by editing sequential chunks, improving on strong baselines across knowledge-editing benchmarks.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether a code assistant can produce working code while being steered toward security flaws. Its attack, INSEC, places a short malicious comment inside the input supplied to a completion engine. The attack operates through black-box access, showing that this manipulation can work against services whose internal models are unavailable to the attacker.

INSEC constructs the comment through an optimization process that queries the completion engine, beginning with carefully designed initial candidates. The researchers evaluate the approach on open-source models and commercial services, including the OpenAI API and GitHub Copilot. Their security-focused test cases cover 16 categories of software weakness across five programming languages.

The experiments report an increase of more than 50% in the rate of insecure code generation while preserving functional correctness. This separates two properties developers might otherwise conflate: code can perform its intended function and still be insecure. The authors also report development costs below 10 US dollars on commodity hardware and demonstrate an IDE plug-in that covertly inserts the attack into Copilot.
icml-2025-black-box-adversarial-attacks-.tldr: INSEC uses short injected comments to steer code-completion engines toward insecure code while preserving functionality in the reported tests.

paragraphs: CateKV targets the memory and computation needed when language models process long contexts. Its starting observation is that some attention heads maintain consistent attention patterns across a sequence. The authors identify these heads using an algorithm based on the coefficient of variation, a measure of variability relative to the average.

The method then treats attention heads differently according to their behavior. For consistent heads, it retains only critical token information in the key-value cache, which stores information used by attention during generation. For adaptive heads, it preserves most key-value pairs. This selective approach concentrates compression where the observed consistency makes a smaller cache useful.

On long-context benchmarks, CateKV maintains accuracy comparable to full attention while reducing memory usage by up to a factor of 2.72. It reports 2.18-fold faster decoding for individual inputs and 3.96-fold higher throughput for batches. The paper also examines extensions with existing acceleration methods. The results support adapting cache retention to individual heads rather than assigning every head the same storage policy.
icml-2025-catekv-on-sequential-consisten.tldr: CateKV compresses caches selectively for attention heads with consistent behavior, improving long-context inference efficiency with comparable benchmark accuracy.

paragraphs: CoLA studies how reinforcement learning should control a language model. Instead of using individual output tokens as the actions, it learns a compact latent action space. These learned actions partially influence token prediction, giving a separate policy a way to guide generation through an intermediate representation.

An inverse dynamics model extracts actions conditioned on future tokens. Meanwhile, the pretrained language model is fine-tuned to accept those actions as a language world model. A policy learns to choose actions within it, either by behavior cloning to imitate a standard language model or by reinforcement learning to maximize rewards for a task.

Applied to Llama-3.1-8B, CoLA produces greater semantic diversity than reinforcement learning with token-level actions. It achieves 42.4 on math500 versus a baseline score of 38.2, rising to 68.2 with a Monte Carlo Tree Search variant. The experiments also report improved agent-task performance without degrading pretrained capabilities, and halved computation time for tasks involving reinforcement-learned thinking prompts. These findings support latent actions as a useful control interface for adaptation.
icml-2025-controlling-large-language-mod.tldr: CoLA learns compact latent actions for controlling language models, improving exploration and downstream reinforcement-learning results in its experiments.

paragraphs: Zero-shot coordination means cooperating with a new partner without first training together. This paper examines why learning cooperation on a single task can leave an agent poorly prepared for even similar new tasks. Its central proposal is to vary the environments during training while keeping the training partner fixed.

The resulting approach, Cross-Environment Cooperation, uses reinforcement learning across a distribution of coordination problems. The authors introduce two procedural generators implemented in Jax that can produce billions of solvable challenges. This supplies many different situations in which agents must cooperate, allowing the study to test whether environmental diversity supports more transferable cooperative behavior.

In evaluations involving real people, the approach outperforms competitive baselines both quantitatively and qualitatively. The findings suggest that exposure to varied scenarios encourages general cooperative norms that also work with unfamiliar partners on unfamiliar problems. This provides evidence for a route toward generalist cooperative agents trained without human data, while preserving the paper’s distinction between demonstrated improvements and the broader possibility of human-compatible cooperation.
icml-2025-cross-environment-cooperation-.tldr: Training with one partner across diverse environments helps agents cooperate with new partners and people on new problems.

paragraphs: CursorCore addresses programming assistance that must account for several sources of information at once. A useful suggestion may depend on the current code, the history of changes, and the user’s instructions. The paper builds a framework for integrating these sources across activities such as completion, insertion, and instructional editing.

The work combines evaluation, data generation, and model training. APEval measures how well assistants align with different information sources and assesses the quality of their outputs. Programming-Instruct generates training examples from sources including GitHub and online judge platforms, automatically producing different kinds of messages that arise during programming. The pipeline produces 219,000 samples for fine-tuning multiple models.

The resulting CursorCore model series outperforms other models of comparable size in the reported evaluation. The framework also brings inline chat and automated editing into a shared approach. Its contribution is therefore both a set of coding models and a way to train and evaluate assistants that must respond to the broader programming process, rather than just a local code fragment.
icml-2025-cursorcore-assist-programming-.tldr: CursorCore combines coding history, code context, and instructions through a unified training pipeline and programming-assistance benchmark.

paragraphs: Different language-model requests place different demands on computation and memory. This paper asks whether a mixture of GPU types can serve those requests more cost-effectively than a uniform collection of devices. Its rationale is that GPU types have distinct resource characteristics that can match different portions of a workload.

Through benchmarking, the authors examine three connected decisions: which GPUs to use, how to configure model deployment, and which workloads to assign to each deployment. They then formulate scheduling with mixed-integer linear programming. The scheduler seeks a cost-efficient serving plan while respecting a spending budget and the GPUs actually available at the time.

The proposed approach outperforms both homogeneous and heterogeneous baselines across the evaluated scenarios, including different workload traces, changing GPU availability, and serving multiple models. The findings show that hardware diversity becomes useful through coordinated deployment and assignment decisions. Simply having different devices is only part of the problem; the study identifies planning their use around request demands as a practical source of efficiency.
icml-2025-demystifying-cost-efficiency-i.tldr: Jointly optimizing GPU types, deployment configurations, and workload assignments improves the cost-efficiency of language-model serving in evaluated scenarios.

paragraphs: DiTAR generates speech using continuous representations without first converting speech into discrete tokens. The paper addresses the computational burden and quality difficulties encountered when combining autoregressive generation with diffusion. Its approach divides speech generation into patches and assigns different parts of the work to a language model and a diffusion transformer.

The language model processes aggregated embeddings that summarize patches. Its output then conditions the diffusion transformer, which generates the next patch. This division lets the autoregressive component work with summaries while the diffusion component constructs the patch itself. The authors report that this organization improves the effectiveness of continuous-token autoregression and reduces computational demands.

The paper also introduces an inference-time temperature defined by when noise enters the reverse diffusion ordinary differential equation, providing a control over diversity and determinism. A scaling analysis reports strong scalability, and zero-shot speech experiments achieve state-of-the-art robustness, speaker similarity, and naturalness. Together, these results support patch-based division of work as an effective architecture for continuous speech generation.
icml-2025-ditar-diffusion-transformer-au.tldr: DiTAR combines patch-level autoregression with diffusion to improve the efficiency and quality of continuous speech generation.

paragraphs: Process supervision evaluates intermediate steps, while outcome supervision evaluates the overall result. For reasoning tasks, step-level feedback seems helpful because it identifies which decisions contributed to success. This paper asks whether outcome-only feedback is inherently more statistically difficult, or whether practical performance differences can arise from the algorithms used.

The main theorem states that, under standard data coverage assumptions, reinforcement learning with outcome supervision is no more statistically difficult than with process supervision. The proof uses a new Change of Trajectory Measure Lemma to connect return-based measures over complete trajectories with distribution shifts at individual steps. The data coverage condition is central to the stated result.

A second result applies when a verifier or rollout capability is available: any policy’s advantage function can serve as an optimal process reward model. This establishes a theoretical connection between outcome information and useful intermediate feedback. The findings suggest that observed performance gaps likely reflect algorithmic limitations rather than inherent statistical difficulty, motivating attention to algorithm design alongside the collection of step-level labels.
icml-2025-do-we-need-to-verify-step-by-s.tldr: Under standard data coverage assumptions, outcome supervision is no more statistically difficult than process supervision in the paper’s theoretical analysis.

paragraphs: An idempotent transformation produces no further change when applied again to its own output. This paper develops a way to train neural networks toward that behavior, which is relevant to data transformations such as image generation and augmentation. The aim is for a network’s first output to already be stable under another application.

Using perturbation theory, the authors derive a matrix update that replaces K with 3K squared minus 2K cubed. For linear, single-layer networks, they show that idempotent matrices are fixed points and that attraction occurs only around idempotent points. This establishes a mathematical foundation for the update in the linear setting without asserting global convergence from every starting matrix.

For nonlinear networks, the method becomes a substitute for the gradient associated with the usual idempotency loss, making the training scheme independent of architecture. Experiments with multilayer perceptrons and convolutional networks report substantially lower idempotency error than the canonical gradient approach. The authors also successfully train a generative network using the method with only a simple reconstruction loss.
icml-2025-enforcing-idempotency-in-neura.tldr: A matrix-derived training update helps neural networks become idempotent, reducing repeated-application error across tested architectures.

paragraphs: Time-series forecasting requires recognizing patterns over time and relationships among the series being predicted. The paper focuses on situations with little training data, where spatio-temporal graph networks and time-series foundation models can struggle despite their strengths on larger datasets. FSTLLM is designed to improve forecasting robustness and predictive performance in these few-shot settings.

The framework draws on contextual knowledge already embedded in large language models to support predictions. This brings pretrained model knowledge into a forecasting problem where task-specific observations are scarce. FSTLLM also supports integration with existing forecasting models, allowing the framework to augment their predictive capabilities within the same approach.

Experiments on real-world datasets report consistently superior performance over major baselines by a significant margin, along with adaptability across the evaluated data. The stated contribution is therefore a framework for making forecasting more effective when examples are limited. Its support for existing forecasters also matters practically: the approach can build on forecasting models already used to capture spatial and temporal dependencies.
icml-2025-fstllm-spatio-temporal-llm-for.tldr: FSTLLM uses pretrained language-model knowledge to improve spatio-temporal forecasting when training data are scarce.

paragraphs: ITBench provides a structured way to measure how effectively AI agents perform real-world IT automation tasks. Its initial release covers site reliability engineering, compliance and security operations, and financial operations. The purpose is to make agent capabilities easier to evaluate through repeatable workflows and metrics that researchers can interpret.

The benchmark contains 102 real-world scenarios and supports extension through community contributions. It also supplies a leaderboard and sample agent implementations. By organizing tasks and evaluation together, ITBench gives researchers a common framework for studying where agents succeed and where operational tasks remain difficult.

Agents powered by state-of-the-art models resolve 11.4% of reliability scenarios, 25.2% of compliance and security scenarios, and 25.8% of financial operations scenarios excluding anomaly detection. On financial anomaly detection, they achieve an F1 score of 0.35. These results show substantial room for improvement on the tested tasks. The authors position ITBench as infrastructure that could help advance correct, safe, and fast automation; that broader outcome is an expectation rather than a demonstrated property of the evaluated agents.
icml-2025-itbench-evaluating-ai-agents-a.tldr: ITBench evaluates agents on 102 real-world IT scenarios and finds low resolution rates across its initial operational task areas.

paragraphs: Label distribution learning represents an example with a distribution over labels, allowing ambiguity to remain part of the prediction. Explaining such a model requires accounting for relationships among labels. This paper adapts local, model-agnostic explanation methods, which are mainly designed for single-label predictions, to this richer output structure.

LIMEFLDL introduces a feature attribution distribution matrix to address dependencies between labels and derives an explanation formula for distribution-valued predictions. The authors provide an analytical solution and conditions governing explanation convergence and stability. These components make the explanation procedure itself more transparent by describing how its answers are obtained and when their behavior is controlled.

The work also supplies a feature-selection scoring function and a fidelity metric tailored to this explanation setting. Numerical and human experiments report high fidelity, consistency, and trustworthiness when explaining label distribution models. The contribution combines a method for explaining black-box predictions with mathematical analysis and evaluation tools suited to outputs whose meaning is spread across multiple related labels.
icml-2025-limefldl-a-local-interpretable.tldr: LIMEFLDL adapts local black-box explanations to label distributions, accounting for label dependencies and analyzing explanation stability.

paragraphs: This paper studies experimentation in which a treatment assigned to one unit can affect other units’ outcomes. Its Multi-armed Bandits with Interference formulation tracks performance throughout an experiment. Over T rounds, a learner assigns an arm to each of N units, and each reward can depend on every unit’s assignment.

The model assumes interference weakens with distance between units. Reward functions may otherwise vary arbitrarily over time and across units under adversarial choice. Against the best policy that always uses one fixed arm, the authors establish an optimal expected regret rate proportional to the square root of T, up to logarithmic factors. A switchback policy can achieve this expected rate.

However, the paper shows that switchback regret has high variance and does not benefit from the number of units in the relevant bound. A new clustered randomization policy retains optimal expected regret while providing a high-probability bound that vanishes with N. This distinguishes average performance from reliable performance in individual experiments and shows how clustering can improve the latter.
icml-2025-multi-armed-bandits-with-inter.tldr: A clustered bandit policy handles distance-decaying interference with optimal expected regret and a high-probability bound that improves with more units.

paragraphs: Algorithms for out-of-distribution generalization address different kinds of changes between training and deployment data. Choosing among them becomes difficult when several shifts occur together. OOD-Chameleon asks whether an algorithm selector can learn this choice from dataset characteristics, reducing the need to train candidate models through trial and error.

The proposed proof of concept treats selection as multi-label classification over a set of candidate algorithms. Its training examples are themselves datasets representing varied distribution shifts. The learned selector is then evaluated on its ability to rank algorithms for unseen datasets and shifts using dataset characteristics alone, without first training those candidate models.

Experiments across synthetic, vision, and language tasks show that the selector identifies high-performing algorithms. Inspection also reveals non-trivial decision rules, offering insight into when existing methods are applicable. The paper presents this as evidence that algorithm selection can itself be learned and as a possible route to making better use of available generalization methods, rather than a universal solution to every distribution shift.
icml-2025-ood-chameleon-is-algorithm-sel.tldr: OOD-Chameleon learns to rank generalization algorithms from dataset characteristics without first training the candidate models.

paragraphs: Pfeife addresses models whose memory requirements exceed the capacity of one GPU. It uses pipeline parallelism, which distributes model execution across multiple devices. The paper focuses on making this practical inside PyTorch without requiring users to manually reorganize a model for pipelined execution.

The tool intercepts model execution and automatically parallelizes it. This matters because support for multiple devices is only useful if the model’s computation can be arranged across them. Pfeife also handles non-sequential models, including Stable Diffusion, extending pipelining to structures that the existing tools discussed in the paper do not support.

The evaluation shows that Pfeife can execute large models that otherwise fail to fit on a single device. It also outperforms state-of-the-art tools by up to 22%. That reported maximum is an empirical result, while the broader contribution is transparent access to pipelining for a wider range of PyTorch models. The work links memory feasibility with automation: models can use several devices without the manual parallelization work that would otherwise be required.
icml-2025-pfeife-automatic-pipeline-para.tldr: Pfeife automatically pipelines PyTorch models across devices, supporting oversized and non-sequential models with reported performance gains of up to 22%.

paragraphs: Reaction Graph addresses chemical reactions as a modeling problem involving relationships across molecules. The paper contrasts this with the stronger attention given to recognizing individual molecules and predicting their properties. Its aim is to provide a representation that brings the participants in a reaction and their three-dimensional structures into one framework.

The representation combines the molecular graphs of reactants and products into a unified graph. It captures interatomic relationships relevant to the reaction and incorporates molecular geometry. This gives the model a shared structure for reasoning about the reaction as a whole, with both molecular connections and three-dimensional information available in the representation.

The authors evaluate Reaction Graph on reaction classification, condition prediction, and yield prediction. It achieves the highest accuracy across six datasets in their experiments. These results support the usefulness of a common reaction-level representation across several predictive tasks. The broader motivation is to improve AI modeling of chemistry for discovery in areas such as drug design and materials science, with the reported evidence coming from those prediction benchmarks.
icml-2025-reaction-graph-towards-reactio.tldr: Reaction Graph unifies reactant and product graphs with 3D molecular information, achieving the highest reported accuracy across six reaction datasets.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning learns from existing data when active exploration would be costly or unsafe. Limited data can leave substantial uncertainty about how the environment behaves. Reflect-then-Plan addresses the resulting tension between cautious offline policies and the need to adapt when new observations become available during deployment.

RefPlan expresses planning as Bayesian posterior estimation and maintains a belief over environment dynamics. At deployment, real-time observations update that belief. Planning then incorporates uncertainty by marginalizing over the possible dynamics, meaning it accounts for alternatives represented in the belief. This connects learning about the environment with choosing actions in a single doubly Bayesian approach.

On standard benchmarks, RefPlan significantly improves the performance of conservative offline reinforcement-learning policies. The experiments report robust behavior with limited data and high uncertainty, together with resilience when environment dynamics change. These findings support using deployment observations to revise beliefs and plans rather than relying entirely on a fixed conservative policy. The demonstrated benefits concern empirical flexibility, generalization, and robustness in the evaluated settings.
icml-2025-reflect-then-plan-offline-mode.tldr: RefPlan updates beliefs about environment dynamics during deployment and incorporates that uncertainty into planning, improving offline-policy performance on benchmarks.

paragraphs: RZ-NAS uses a language model to help search for neural network architectures. The paper targets three problems in existing approaches: restricted search spaces, expensive searches, and weak results across benchmarks and downstream tasks. Its proposal combines language-model reflection with metrics that evaluate candidate architectures without training them.

Structured prompts help the language model interpret both the search task and candidate architectures through their text and code. Reflection modules then produce feedback in natural language to guide architecture optimization. The training-free metrics provide another source of guidance, allowing the search to assess candidates without the extensive training costs associated with direct performance evaluation.

The authors report effective searches in both micro and macro search spaces, covering choices at different architectural scales. They also report state-of-the-art performance across multiple downstream tasks without extensive search time. The contribution is a coordinated search strategy in which generated feedback and inexpensive evaluation support architecture refinement. Here, zero-cost refers to the training-free metrics; the framework still performs a search involving prompts, candidate architectures, and feedback.
icml-2025-rz-nas-enhancing-llm-guided-ne.tldr: RZ-NAS combines language-model reflection with training-free metrics to guide efficient architecture searches across multiple search spaces.

paragraphs: SADA accelerates diffusion and flow-matching generation while aiming to keep outputs faithful to the unmodified model. The authors hypothesize that earlier methods lose fidelity because denoising trajectories vary with prompts and because their approximations overlook the numerical solution of the underlying ordinary differential equation.

The method uses one stability criterion to coordinate sparsity decisions across both sampling steps and tokens. It adjusts sparsity to the actual sampling trajectory and constructs approximations using precise gradient information from the numerical solver. This connects decisions about reducing computation to the evolving generation process and the solver used to follow it.

Evaluations on SD-2, SDXL, and Flux with EDM and DPM++ solvers report consistent speedups of at least 1.8 times, with LPIPS at most 0.10 and FID at most 4.5 relative to unmodified baselines. The method also accelerates ControlNet without modifications and achieves a 1.8-fold speedup on MusicLDM with approximately 0.01 spectrogram LPIPS. These experiments support the approach across multiple image pipelines and an audio-generation setting.
icml-2025-sada-stability-guided-adaptive.tldr: SADA uses numerical stability to adapt step and token sparsity, delivering reported speedups of at least 1.8 times with small fidelity losses.

paragraphs: Predicting flow on a directed graph requires distinguishing the direction of its connections. The paper identifies a difficulty for graph neural networks: they can fail to preserve high-frequency components of signals on nodes. These components describe detailed variation that matters for flow dynamics, and losing them can make forward and reversed graph structures appear equivalent.

The proposed framework combines two mechanisms. Explicit difference matrices model directional gradients, making changes along directed connections available to the model. Implicit physical constraints guide message passing so that information exchanged within the graph neural network remains consistent with natural laws. Together, these mechanisms aim to preserve sensitivity to detailed differences in topology.

The authors evaluate the framework on real-world water flux and urban traffic flow networks and report that it is effective. These two applications connect the architectural motivation to systems where direction is central to flow prediction. The contribution is a way to combine explicit directional information with physics-guided learning so that the network can better distinguish graph structures that imply different flow behavior.
icml-2025-topology-aware-neural-flux-pre.tldr: Directional difference matrices and physical constraints help graph neural networks capture topology relevant to water and traffic flow prediction.

paragraphs: This paper studies memorization in diffusion models through the geometry of their probability landscapes. It focuses on the sharpness of log probability density: how sharply the modeled density changes around a location. This provides a mathematical lens for analyzing memorization and for interpreting signals used to detect it.

The authors mathematically justify an existing memorization metric based on score differences by showing that it quantifies sharpness. They then introduce a new metric that measures sharpness at the beginning of image generation in latent diffusion models. The timing matters because the metric offers an early indication of potential memorization while generation is still at its initial stage.

The proposed mitigation strategy uses this early signal to optimize the initial noise from which generation begins. A sharpness-aware regularization term guides that optimization, connecting the geometric analysis directly to an intervention in the generation process. The paper thus links an explanation of an existing metric, a new early-stage metric, and a method intended to reduce memorization through the starting noise.
icml-2025-understanding-and-mitigating-m.tldr: The paper links diffusion-model memorization to probability sharpness and uses an early sharpness signal to guide initial-noise optimization.

paragraphs: Verification Learning asks when neuro-symbolic systems can learn without labeled examples. Removing labels leaves fewer clues about symbols, more possible solutions, and opportunities for shortcuts. The proposed approach replaces label-based reasoning with a verification function that checks whether current predictions satisfy rules, using that feedback together with unlabeled data.

The authors formulate learning as a constraint optimization problem. Their Dynamic Combinatorial Sorting algorithm reduces the number of verification attempts needed, lowering computational costs. A separate prior alignment method addresses potential shortcuts. These components tackle both the difficulty of searching through possible predictions and the risk that a rule-compatible solution may exploit an unintended shortcut.

The theoretical analysis distinguishes tasks for which rules can replace unlimited labels from tasks for which the rules provide no benefit. That distinction is central: label-free learning depends on what the rules can establish for the particular task. Experiments on fully unsupervised addition, sorting, matching, and chess tasks report significant improvements in performance and efficiency, supporting the framework in those tested settings.
icml-2025-verification-learning-make-uns.tldr: Verification Learning trains neuro-symbolic systems from unlabeled data and rule checks, while analyzing which tasks can benefit from replacing labels with rules.

paragraphs: Federated learning combines training across clients without requiring them to share their local data. A central difficulty is that clients may hold data from different distributions, making their learning problems heterogeneous. This paper examines how neural network width changes the impact of that heterogeneity on FedAvg trained with gradient descent.

The theoretical analysis shows that the effect of data heterogeneity diminishes as network width increases and vanishes in the infinite-width limit. In that limit, both local client models and the global model behave as linear models. The authors further prove that FedAvg matches the generalization performance of centralized learning when both use the same number of gradient-descent iterations.

Experiments across different network architectures, loss functions, and optimization methods support the theoretical findings. The key implication is that model width can influence how strongly differences among client datasets affect learning. The exact equivalence with centralized learning belongs to the infinite-width regime, while the broader result identifies widening as a way to mitigate heterogeneity rather than asserting that every finite network eliminates it.
icml-2025-widening-the-network-mitigates.tldr: The analysis shows that widening networks reduces heterogeneity’s impact on FedAvg, with centralized-learning equivalence established in the infinite-width regime.

paragraphs: Cyclic peptides have geometric constraints that linear peptides do not, creating a challenge for generative design when cyclic training examples are scarce. CP-Composer addresses this by learning reusable geometric constraints from linear peptides and combining them to generate cyclic structures targeted toward binding.

The framework decomposes complex cyclization patterns into simpler unit constraints. A diffusion model receives these constraints through geometric conditioning on nodes and edges. During training, it sees unit constraints and random combinations within linear peptides. At inference, it receives new combinations that impose the requirements for cyclization, allowing the desired geometry to be specified through composed constraints.

Experiments show that a model trained on linear peptides can generate diverse target-binding cyclic peptides, with success rates ranging from 38% to 84% across different cyclization strategies. The zero-shot result concerns applying learned constraints in new combinations required for cyclic design. It supports compositional geometry as a way to transfer from available linear-peptide training data to a design setting with limited dedicated data.
icml-2025-zero-shot-cyclic-peptide-desig.tldr: CP-Composer combines geometric constraints learned from linear peptides to generate target-binding cyclic peptides without cyclic-peptide training.
